message.reasoning_content:
The user wants a translation of Java code to C++.
The Java code reads an integer `n` and a string `t`.
It iterates `i` from 2 to `n`.
If `n % i == 0`, it reverses the prefix of `t` of length `i` and appends the rest of the string.
Then updates `t` to this new string.
Finally prints `t`.

Key differences Java vs C++:
- Scanner -> cin
- String concatenation `+=` works similarly in C++ `std::string`.
- `charAt` -> `[]` or `at()`.
- `substring` -> `substr`.
- `System.out.println` -> `cout << ... << endl;`
- Need includes: `<iostream>`, `<string>`.

Algorithm check:
Input: n, t.
Loop i from 2 to n.
If n % i == 0:
  Reverse t[0...i-1].
  Keep t[i...end].
  Update t.

Example: n=10, t="abcdefghij"
Divisors of 10: 2, 5, 10.
i=2: reverse "ab" -> "ba", rest "cdefghij" -> "bacdefghij"
i=5: reverse "bacde" -> "edcab", rest "fghij" -> "edcabfghij"
i=10: reverse whole string -> "jihgfabcde"
Output: "jihgfabcde"

C++ implementation:
Use `std::string t;`
Loop `for (int i = 2; i <= n; ++i)`
Inside: `if (n % i == 0)`
Reverse prefix: `std::reverse(t.begin(), t.begin() + i);`
Wait, the Java code does:
`s += t.charAt(j)` for j from i-1 down to 0. This builds reversed prefix.
`s += t.substring(i)` appends rest.
`t = s`.

In C++, `std::reverse(t.begin(), t.begin() + i);` modifies `t` in place. This is equivalent and more efficient.
However, to be strictly faithful to the logic (though `std::reverse` is standard C++), I'll use `std::reverse`.

Headers: `<bits/stdc++.h>` or `<iostream>`, `<string>`, `<algorithm>`.
Main function.
`std::ios_base::sync_with_stdio(false); std::cin.tie(NULL);` for speed.

Code structure:
```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <algorithm>

int main() {
    std::ios_base::sync_with_stdio(false);
    std::cin.tie(NULL);

    int n;
    std::string t;
    std::cin >> n >> t;

    for (int i = 2; i <= n; ++i) {
        if (n % i == 0) {
            std::reverse(t.begin(), t.begin() + i);
        }
    }

    std::cout << t << std::endl;
    return 0;
}
```
This looks correct and idiomatic C++.

source_data.prob_desc_description: A string $$$s$$$ of length $$$n$$$ can be encrypted by the following algorithm:  iterate over all divisors of $$$n$$$ in decreasing order (i.e. from $$$n$$$ to $$$1$$$),  for each divisor $$$d$$$, reverse the substring $$$s[1 \dots d]$$$ (i.e. the substring which starts at position $$$1$$$ and ends at position $$$d$$$). For example, the above algorithm applied to the string $$$s$$$="codeforces" leads to the following changes: "codeforces" $$$\to$$$ "secrofedoc" $$$\to$$$ "orcesfedoc" $$$\to$$$ "rocesfedoc" $$$\to$$$ "rocesfedoc" (obviously, the last reverse operation doesn't change the string because $$$d=1$$$).You are given the encrypted string $$$t$$$. Your task is to decrypt this string, i.e., to find a string $$$s$$$ such that the above algorithm results in string $$$t$$$. It can be proven that this string $$$s$$$ always exists and is unique.
source_data.prob_desc_output_spec: Print a string $$$s$$$ such that the above algorithm results in $$$t$$$.
source_data.prob_desc_input_spec: The first line of input consists of a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 100$$$) — the length of the string $$$t$$$. The second line of input consists of the string $$$t$$$. The length of $$$t$$$ is $$$n$$$, and it consists only of lowercase Latin letters.
source_data.prob_desc_notes: NoteThe first example is described in the problem statement.
